title: Asalha again
hook: the first sermon, heard a fourth year

segments.voice: Yesterday, Poson and a tracker following footprints, with one line: who brought it.

How does a sermon end? Usually, people stand up and go home. The first sermon ends differently. In the Deer Park near Benares, the Buddha finishes speaking to five ascetics, and the sutta turns its camera upward. The gods of the earth hear it and shout: the wheel has been set rolling, and nobody in the world can turn it back. The gods above them hear the shout and pass it on, heaven after heaven, all the way up. The whole world system trembles, and a great light appears. You've heard this sermon on Asalha's full moon before: the middle way, the four truths. This fourth time, listen for a quieter pattern inside it.
screen: `A SERMON IN THE DEER PARK.` → `THE SHOUT GOES UP.` → `A PATTERN INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the four truths, short. There is suffering. It has a cause, craving. It can end. And there's a path to its ending. Now the pattern. In the sutta, the Buddha doesn't just name each truth; he walks around each one three times. This is suffering; suffering is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood. This is the cause; it is to be let go; it has been let go. This is the ending; it is to be seen for yourself; it has been seen. This is the path; it is to be walked; it has been walked. Each truth gets a different job: understand, let go, see, walk. Suffering isn't something you abandon; it's something you understand. Craving isn't something you study forever; it's something you set down. Why did this matter? In the sutta, he says that until his knowing was clear in all these ways, he didn't claim to be fully awake. Only when he'd walked around every truth did he say it. Then the wheel. The sermon's title is the setting in motion of the wheel of the teaching. A wheel is something you push once, and then it rolls. In Theravada lands, the Asalha full moon keeps that first push in memory, and the next day the rains retreat traditionally begins. Each year the wheel is heard again, and each year someone hears it as if for the first time.
screen: `FOUR TRUTHS, SHORT.` · `EACH TRUTH, THREE TIMES.` · `UNDERSTAND, LET GO, SEE, WALK.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Say the sermon's outline silently, one line per breath: there is suffering, to be understood; there is a cause, to be let go; there is an ending, to be seen; there is a path, to be walked. Say it again, slower, and the third time let each line touch one small, real thing in your day: a sore back, a craving for your phone, a moment of quiet, a step you could take. Then let the words go and sit with the breath.
Asalha. The full moon that remembers the first sermon in the Deer Park, when the wheel of the teaching was set rolling. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel turns. One push, and it keeps on rolling. See you on the next turn.

howItsDone: On the Asalha full moon, Theravada Buddhists visit temples, listen to or chant the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, keep extra precepts, and often walk around the temple holding candles, flowers and incense.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first sermon is a list of four truths.
what it means: four truths, each walked around three times, each with its own job: understand, let go, see, walk.

chat.says: Isn't Buddhism just about getting rid of suffering as fast as you can?
options: In the first sermon, suffering is to be understood; it's craving that's to be let go.
Yes. The first sermon says to abandon suffering, and the path is how you do it.
No. The sermon says suffering is good for you, so you should seek out more.
chat.meaning: In the first sermon the Buddha gives each truth its own job: suffering to be understood, its cause let go, its ending seen, the path walked.

notes: SN 56.11 paraphrased throughout, including the three rounds of each truth (sacca-ñana, kicca-ñana, kata-ñana), the four tasks (pariññeyya, pahatabba, sacchikatabba, bhavetabba), the Buddha not claiming awakening until his knowledge was purified in these ways, and the gods' cry rising through the heavens with the world system trembling and a great light.
